records.content_title: Lehigh Valley confirms 1st measles case amid nation’s worst year for virus in decades
records.content: Health officials this week confirmed the Lehigh Valley's first measles case amid a rise in infections across Pennsylvania and the United States. St. Luke's University Health Network announced Monday night it is treating its first case of the highly contagious disease in recent memory. It is a pediatric case, the network said. "Measles cases are on the rise in the United States, but we now have our first case here in the region," Dr. Jennifer Janco, a St. Luke's pediatrician, said in a video update released by the network . St. Luke's spokesman Sam Kennedy clarified Tuesday the network is treating two patients with measles, both pediatric cases in Lehigh County of siblings who tested positive. One was receiving inpatient treatment, and the other was recovering at home. The infections come as Pennsylvania experiences an increase in measles cases , bringing a national health concern to local communities. Health officials are now urging residents to check their vaccination status and get vaccinated if needed. Janco, chairwoman of the St. Luke's Pediatric Department, emphasized the serious nature of the virus. "Measles is one of the most contagious diseases that we know of. You only need to be around the airspace, not the person, and it can linger in the air," she explained. The virus poses a significant threat to unprotected individuals, Janco said: "Nine out of 10 people who aren't protected are going to contract measles if they're exposed." The disease can lead to severe health complications requiring hospitalization. Janco warned that measles can cause swelling of the brain and affect the lungs. The risks extend beyond immediate illness, as the virus can create ongoing health problems for survivors. The number of measles cases in the U.S. in July surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025 , with five more months of 2026 still to come. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it logged 2,318 cases of measles as of July 23. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades. Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.'s worst year for measles since 1991, as major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona have sickened hundreds and smaller clusters of cases sparked in other states. A Pennsylvania Department of Health dashboard of measles infections statewide shows 176 cases as of Monday, including the two in Lehigh County and seven in neighboring counties — three in Montgomery and four in Berks. Despite concerns of an outbreak, health officials stress that measles is preventable through vaccination. The cases are affecting children in the region, but Janco pointed to an effective solution. "The good news is we can prevent measles cases. So, yes, we are seeing cases in children, but we have a very powerful prevention tool in the form of vaccination," she said. St. Luke's advises parents with unvaccinated children to contact their pediatrician immediately to schedule vaccinations. Many adults may also need protection, and the health network urges certain adult populations to verify their vaccination status. "People born between 1963 and 1967 may have had an older version of the vaccine and might benefit from today's updated version," Janco explained. Additionally, adults vaccinated during childhood may not have received adequate protection. "If you were vaccinated before 1991, you may have only received one dose because that's what the recommendation was then," she said. The current medical recommendation calls for two doses of the measles vaccine. Janco stressed the effectiveness of the complete vaccination series. "We know two doses of the vaccine is a powerful protection tool and we are not seeing cases of measles in vaccinated persons," she said. Those unsure about their vaccination status should consult with their healthcare provider to determine if they need vaccination or additional doses, health officials stressed. Lehigh Valley Health Network, part of Jefferson Health , is also on the alert for measles, with a spokesperson telling lehighvalleylive.com: "The Pennsylvania Department of Health notified us of two confirmed cases of measles locally, following the evaluation of a patient at Lehigh Valley Reilly Children's Hospital. "Appropriate precautions were implemented as soon as measles was suspected, and we will continue to work closely with state health officials." The Associated Press contributed to this report. The Collection Riverpark mall in Oxnard (above) includes Cinemark Century Riverpark movie theater, one of the locations visited by the individual who was later positively diagnosed with measles. | Credit: Drewrx/Wikimedia Commons A case of measles in an individual who had been traveling internationally was announced on August 5 by Ventura County, the county just south of Santa Barbara. Identifying information is not available due to medical privacy rules, but Ventura’s public health contact tracers put together a list of places the individual was known to be before being positively diagnosed: • July 26: Subway, 1941 N. Rose Ave., Suite 600, Oxnard (approx. 8 –10 a.m.) • July 27-August 1: Hacienda Furniture and Mattress, 3200 S. Saviers Rd., Oxnard • July 31: Cinemark Century Riverpark, 2766 Seaglass Way, Oxnard (approx. 7:30 p.m.–midnight) • August 1: Walgreens, 1801 N. Rose Ave., Oxnard (approx. 9:30–11 a.m.) • August 2: Kaiser Permanente, 4949 Market St., Ventura (approx. 9–11 a.m.) With measles, it can take a week or two before symptoms appear, which at first are usually a high fever, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. A rash starts about 3-5 days after those symptoms appear, generally at the hairline and descending from there. Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through airborne particles brought up by coughing and sneezing. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves a room. Ventura County has strong vaccination rates, said the county’s public health officer, Dr. Uldine Castel, and hasn’t had a measles case since 2017. Similarly, Santa Barbara County has a greater than 95 percent measles vaccination rate and has not had a measles case since 2019. People who have been vaccinated or were born before 1957 are generally considered at a low risk. The risk increases for those who’ve never had measles, have not been vaccinated, or are immunocompromised. (AP: Jose Luis Magana) In short: US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr says parents should vaccinate their children against measles. The advice from the longtime vaccine critic comes amid the worst outbreak in 35 years. What's next? International health officials will meet later this year to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has urged parents to vaccinate their children following a record-breaking measles outbreak in the United States. Mr Kennedy, a longtime vaccine critic who has regularly told Americans they should not take medical advice from him, warned people to get the jab during a heated interview on CNN on Sunday, local time. “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles," he said. "A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97 per cent of the cases. People should get vaccinated.” The rise in measles, declared essentially eradicated in the US a quarter of a century ago, has been linked by medical experts to slumping immunisation rates, a trend many attribute in part to vaccine scepticism espoused by Mr Kennedy. More than 2,370 cases of measles have been confirmed in the US this year, already breaking last year's multi-decade high. RFK Jr defended his handling of the measles outbreak in the interview with Dana Bash. (Supplied) During the CNN interview, Mr Kennedy was asked if he took any responsibility for the measles surge. “Absolutely not,” he said. Mr Kennedy later went on to accuse CNN host Dana Bash of "repeating like a parrot" and becoming "flustered". Worst year for measles in decades Many health officials have cited a public backlash to the government's pandemic response and blame Mr Kennedy's anti-vaccine policies for further undermining trust in immunisations. "The whole thing about 'vaccines have been tested and there's been this determination made' is just a lie," Mr Kennedy said in a 2025 interview. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the most since 1991. This year there have been major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona, as well as smaller clusters in other states. International health officials will meet in November to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The US eliminated the local spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but in recent years they have fallen below the 95 per cent coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Measles cases under-counted Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts of disease cases are incomplete because not everyone seeks treatment. Measles testing was conducted in Texas in 2025 (Reuters: Sebastian Rocandio) Experts suspect the spread of measles cases may be wider than has been reported due to the decline in vaccination rates. National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5 per cent among kindergarteners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2 per cent in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities. In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has struck more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department. Experts relying on mathematical modelling and genetic analyses indicate that a large outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be three to four times bigger than what is known, according to Utah state epidemiologist Leisha Nolen. records.content: News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL Health officials confirm two measles cases in Wayne County Staff Report Aug. 5, 2026, 4:28 p.m. ET The Wayne County Health Department said the exposure possibly happened at Smokey Lane Stables in Sugarcreek on July 17. There is an additional suspected case being investigated. WOOSTER — Two cases of measles have been confirmed in Wayne County, according to the health department. The Wayne County Health Department received laboratory confirmation and is working closely with the OhioDepartment of Health to identify and notify anyone who may have been exposed. The cases are likely associated with the previously announced measles exposure at Smokey Lane Stables in Sugarcreek on July 17, according to the announcement. The individuals were exposed during that event and later developed symptoms consistent with measles. This marks the first confirmed measles cases in Wayne County residents associated with that potential exposure. There is an additional suspected case being investigated. “We are actively monitoring Wayne County residents who may have been exposed. We are asking residents to be aware of symptoms and to take precautions when seeking treatment. Without a doubt, being vaccinated against the measles virus still offers the best protection. It is safe and it works, “ said Wayne County Health Commissioner Nicholas Cascarelli in a news release. Contact the Wayne County Health Department at (330) 264-9590 if you have questions about measles or for times and locations of upcoming vaccine clinics throughout Wayne County. Measles can be especially dangerous for babies or young children. It spreads through the air when a sick person coughs or sneezes. The virus can stay in the air for two hours after a person with measles leaves the space. The best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, according to the health department. Anyone who is not vaccinated is at risk of measles infection and severe complications. Measles symptoms appear 7 to 14 days after contact with the virus. Common symptoms include: High fever (may spike to more than 104°F) Cough Runny nose Red and/or watery eyes Rash (breaks out 3-5 days after symptoms begin) Measles can cause severe health problems, including: Pneumonia Swelling of the brain (encephalitis) Possibly even death If someone in your family has measles symptoms: Keep them away from family members who are not sick. Everyone in the house should stay home to not get your neighbors or people outside of yourhome sick. Call a doctor or hospital right away to let them know someone in your home may be sick withmeasles. They will give you instructions. When to go to the emergency room: If the person who is sick gets rapidly worse, or has any of the symptoms listed below, take them to theemergency department of a hospital immediately. Do not wait, the health department states. Trouble breathing (or breathing faster than normal) Pain when breathing or coughing Dehydration (dry nose and mouth, urinating less, crying without making tears) Fever or headache that will not stop Confusion, decreased alertness, or severe weakness Blue color around the mouth, low energy, or difficulty feeding (for young children) Have someone call before you arrive, and stay in your car. Read Full Bio Chelsea Hylton August 6, 2026 / 11:28 AM PDT / CBS LA Add CBS News on Google A measles exposure warning was issued at Universal Studios Hollywood on Wednesday after a visitor tested positive for the disease, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health said. Public health officials said there was a confirmed case of measles in a person who was infectious while they visited the theme park on July 26. Anyone who was at Universal Studios Hollywood on the same day from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. may have been exposed. LA County Public Health urges that people who were at the location during that time frame may be at risk of developing measles from 7 to 21 days after being exposed. They should confirm if they are vaccinated against measles, contact and notify their healthcare provider and call a healthcare provider immediately if symptoms develop. People who have had measles in the past or have received the recommended measles vaccine are likely protected from the disease but should still monitor for symptoms. People who are unimmunized or have unknown measles immunization status are at higher risk and they should monitor for symptoms closely. Public health officials say anyone who remains symptom-free for more than 21 days after being exposed is no longer considered at risk. The last day to monitor for symptoms is August 16, 2026. "Getting vaccinated is the best way to protect yourself and your family from getting measles," LA County Public Health says. According to LA County Public Health, the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR or MMRV, is 95% effective after two doses and 93% effective after one. Public health staff said anyone who does not develop symptoms after 21 days is no longer considered at risk of contracting measles. Common symptoms for measles include: High fever (higher than 101° F) Cough Runny nose Red and watery eyes Rash 3-5 days after other signs of illness. The "measles rash" typically starts on the face and then spreads down to the rest of the body According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been more than 2,300 confirmed cases of measles in the U.S. in 2026. In California, there are nearly 50 confirmed cases. For questions or to find a nearby clinic or doctor, call the Public Health InfoLine at 833-540-0473. records.content: TRUMBULL COUNTY, Ohio — The Trumbull County Combined Health District is investigating two confirmed measles cases within the county this week. Health officials said the two individuals were unvaccinated and the cases were unrelated. Officials said one of the individuals, during the infectious period, was present at: - Walmart: 200 Goldie Road in Liberty on July 29 - Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department: 6505 Market St. in Boardman on Aug. 2 TCCHD is working alongside Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department and the Ohio Department of Health to investigate and notify anyone potentially exposed. The health district recommends contacting a doctor if you're unsure of your vaccination status and were within the exposed areas; those unvaccinated should monitor themselves for signs and symptoms of measles for 21 days after exposure. Measles, which is extremely contagious, is spread through sneezing and coughing. The virus can live up to two hours in the air where the infected person coughed or sneezed. Once breathed in, an individual can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Symptoms include: - Rash - High fever - Running nose - Cough - Loss of appetite - Red, watery eyes Senior digital producer Lydia Taylor contributed to this report

records.content: Stock photo of a person with the measles. (Mumemories/Getty Images) (NEW YORK) — Los Angeles County health officials said a person infected with measles visited Universal Studios Hollywood last month and potentially exposed others to the virus. The county’s Department of Public Health said Wednesday that it is investigating the case involving the visitor who was at the theme park on July 26. Other possible locations within the county are being probed, according to the health department. Anyone who was in the park that day between 10 a.m. and 9 p.m. is asked to confirm their protection against the virus and is warned that they may be at risk of developing measles from seven to 21 days after being exposed, according to the health department. Health officials said that people who have been vaccinated against the virus are likely to be protected, as are people who had measles previously. “People who are unimmunized or have unknown measles immunization status are at higher risk and should monitor for symptoms closely. Anyone who remains symptom-free for more than 21 days after being exposed is no longer considered at risk,” the health department said in a statement. A spokesperson for Universal Studios Hollywood said in a statement Friday that the park is working with the health department in their probe. “The safety and security of our guests and team members is our highest priority,” the company said. Measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes or a rash. The virus can spread through the air and can remain in the air or on infected surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Anyone who believes they have contracted measles is urged to call a doctor immediately, according to the health department. “Measles spreads easily and can lead to serious complications, including pneumonia, brain swelling, and even death,” Dr. Muntu Davis, the Los Angeles County Health Officer, said in a statement. Over 2,300 measles cases have been recorded this year, the highest number since 1991, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The majority of measles cases in 2026 have been confirmed among children and teenagers aged 19 and younger, according to the CDC. About one in 10 children under age 5 diagnosed with measles this year have been hospitalized. About 93% of cases this year are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says. -ABC News’ Mary Kekatos contributed to this report. Copyright Â© 2026, ABC Audio. All rights reserved
